960.title: Exile in Burma
960.hook: Baba Ram Singh was exiled to Rangoon
960.howItsDone: Namdhari Sikhs remember Baba Ram Singh's exile to Burma, keep letters they hold he wrote from there, and Namdhari tradition looks for his return.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Malerkotla, and a line about remembering. Today, what happened to the teacher himself.

A ship pulls away from the coast of India, heading east across the Bay of Bengal. On board, under guard, is a man in white who has never been tried for any crime. He's being taken to Rangoon, in Burma, where he doesn't speak the language, far from his village, his people and the fields of the Punjab. The British have decided to keep Baba Ram Singh far from anyone who might gather around him.
screen: `A SHIP HEADING EAST.` → `A MAN IN WHITE, UNDER GUARD.` → `NEVER TRIED.` → `RANGOON, FAR FROM THE PUNJAB.`

segments.voice: First, the arrest. After Malerkotla, the British took Baba Ram Singh into custody, though Namdhari histories say he hadn't sent the raiders. He wasn't put on trial. The government used an old regulation that let it hold a person as a state prisoner without charges, and sent him far from the Punjab, across the sea. Second, the place. Burma was then ruled from British India, and Rangoon was its port city. For a teacher whose whole life was a village, a congregation and the Name recited together, this was very far from home. He was kept under watch, with few of his own people allowed near. Third, the letters. Namdharis keep letters said to have been written by Baba Ram Singh in exile and carried back to the Punjab. In them, the community remembers, he encouraged his followers to hold to the Name and to their discipline. Exile cut the road, but not every thread. Fourth, the end, and who says what. British records say he died in Burma. Namdhari tradition holds that he did not die there, and looks for his return. That belief belongs to the Namdhari community, and this lesson simply reports it. Punjabi has a word for the one far from home: pardesi, the traveler in a strange land. Some readers of the Guru's hymns hear the soul itself pictured that way, a guest in this world, longing for home. Baba Ram Singh lived that picture in his body.
screen: `HELD WITHOUT TRIAL.` · `RANGOON, A PORT FAR EAST.` · `LETTERS CARRIED HOME.` · `WHO SAYS WHAT ABOUT THE END.` · then, large: `FAR FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who lives far from home, not by choice: a refugee, a prisoner, someone who can't go back; you don't need their name. Picture them waking somewhere strange today, and on each breath out, wish them one thing: safety, a letter from home, a familiar voice. If you pray, hold them before Waheguru in the quiet.
Pardesi, the one far from home, a traveler in a strange land: Baba Ram Singh, held without trial, sent to Rangoon, remembered by his followers through his letters. Today's word.
Your line: far from home. Far away, and still holding the Name. Day nine hundred sixty.

961.title: Amritsar's Singh Sabha, 1873
961.hook: Sikhs in Amritsar formed a society to renew teaching, schools and literature
961.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Singh Sabha of Amritsar as the start of a renewal of Sikh teaching, schools and Punjabi books; study circles and gurdwara classes carry on that work today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pardesi: Baba Ram Singh, held far from home in Rangoon. Today, back in the Punjab, people start to gather.

A room in Amritsar. A group of Sikh gentlemen sit together, worried. The kingdom is gone. The old schools are thin. Printed books in Punjabi are hard to find. And news has come that some Sikh students at a mission school plan to leave the faith. Nobody in the room has an army. What they have is a meeting, and by the end of it, they've founded a society with a plain name.
screen: `A ROOM IN AMRITSAR.` → `THE KINGDOM IS GONE.` → `NO ARMY, ONLY A MEETING.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Singh, the lion, is the name Khalsa men take. Sabha means an assembly or society. So Singh Sabha is simply the society of the Singhs, a gathering of Sikhs with a purpose. Second, the worry. After the loss of the kingdom, Sikh leaders saw learning slipping away. Histories say the spark included word that a few Sikh students at a Christian mission school were about to be baptized. Missionaries were active in the Punjab and debated in the open. The founders' answer, as the histories tell it, was to turn inward: to teach their own young people their own Gurus. Third, what they set out to do. Renew Sikh teaching as the Gurus gave it. Open schools. Print books and papers in Punjabi, in the Gurmukhi letters. Welcome back those who had drifted away. And, under British rule, seek the goodwill of officials for their schools. Fourth, why a meeting matters. In a hymn in Sri Rag, Guru Nanak asks how the true congregation is recognized, and answers: it's where the One Name is spoken. The Singh Sabha was a congregation for a new age, not a court or a camp, but people sitting together to study and teach. In the years that followed, other Singh Sabhas sprang up in other towns, and tomorrow you'll meet a bolder one. Renewal, here, begins in a room with a few chairs.

See the first ten minutes: one reads, the others listen, someone asks a question. If you pray, ask in your own words for a good sangat, the company of seekers.

962.title: The Lahore Sabha, 1879
962.hook: a bolder reform society formed in Lahore
962.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the Lahore Singh Sabha for its plain insistence, in Punjabi papers and pamphlets, that all Sikhs stand equal before the Guru whatever their birth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Singh Sabha: a room in Amritsar, and renewal beginning. Today, a second Sabha, in a second city, with a sharper voice.

Lahore, the old capital of Ranjit Singh's kingdom, is now a British city of colleges, printing presses and newspapers. A young teacher at a college there, and a circle of friends around him, have been watching the Amritsar Sabha. They agree with its aims. But they think it's too polite. Too careful with old privileges. Too slow to say plainly what the Gurus said. So they start their own.
screen: `LAHORE, A CITY OF PRESSES.` → `A YOUNG TEACHER AND HIS FRIENDS.` → `TOO POLITE, TOO SLOW.`

segments.voice: First, who they were. The Lahore Singh Sabha gathered teachers, clerks and writers, people who lived by books and print. Professor Gurmukh Singh was among its leaders, and Giani Ditt Singh, a writer you'll meet tomorrow, joined it. Second, what they said out loud. All Sikhs are equal before the Guru, whatever family they were born into. No one is owed special honor in the sangat for descending from a Guru's family. Caste has no place at the Guru's door. In a hymn in Sri Rag, Guru Nanak says he stands with the lowest of the low, and has no wish to vie with the great. The Lahore reformers took that line at its word. Third, the clash. The Amritsar leaders included men of honored lineages, some descended from the Gurus' own families, who held that old customs and old respect deserved a place. The Lahore group thought this blurred the Gurus' teaching. The two Sabhas formed rival councils, and their disagreement was public and sometimes bitter. Each side believed it was protecting the Panth. Historians still weigh both sides, and this lesson leaves the judging to them. Fourth, the tool. The Lahore reformers spoke clearly in print: papers and pamphlets in Punjabi, passed from hand to hand. A sentence on a page could travel further than a speech in a hall. Speaking clearly isn't shouting. It means saying the thing plainly, so nobody has to guess what you meant.
screen: `TEACHERS, CLERKS AND WRITERS.` · `ALL EQUAL BEFORE THE GURU.` · `TWO SABHAS, TWO COUNCILS.` · `SPEAKING CLEARLY IN PRINT.` · then, large: `SPEAK CLEARLY.`

segments.voice: Think of something that matters to you that you've been saying in a roundabout way, or not at all: a need, a thanks, a boundary. Let the extra words fall away one by one until a single plain sentence is left, and breathe with it; it doesn't need to be sharp, just clear. If you pray, rest in Waheguru between the breaths.
Sabha, an assembly or society: the bolder Lahore Singh Sabha, which said plainly in print that all Sikhs stand equal before the Guru. Today's word.
Your line: speak clearly. Plain words, kindly said, travel far. That's day nine hundred sixty-two.

963.title: Giani Ditt Singh
963.hook: a scholar from a family counted low became a leading Sikh writer
963.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Giani Ditt Singh as a writer and editor of the Singh Sabha reform who rose from a family counted low, and the title Giani is still given to those learned in the Gurus' word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sabha: the bolder Lahore Sabha, saying plainly that all Sikhs are equal before the Guru. Today, one of the clearest voices it had.

In a Punjab village, a boy is born into a family the caste order counts low. People like him are expected to work with their hands, keep their eyes down, and leave books to others. This boy doesn't. He learns to read. He learns poetry and argument. He studies with one religious teacher after another, asking hard questions. And one day, in Lahore, he's editing a Sikh newspaper in Punjabi. He's called Giani, the learned one.
screen: `A FAMILY COUNTED LOW.` → `A BOY WHO LEARNS TO READ.` → `EDITING A SIKH NEWSPAPER.`

segments.voice: First, the title. Giani means a learned one. In Sikh life it's a title for a person learned in the Gurus' word and able to explain it. Nobody is born a Giani; it's earned with years of study. Second, the search. Before he took the Khalsa's amrit, Ditt Singh moved through more than one religious circle, listening, reading, testing. He came to the Gurus' path as a thinker who had looked around, not as someone who'd never been asked. Third, the work. In Lahore he joined the Singh Sabha and became one of its sharpest writers. He edited the Khalsa Akhbar, a Punjabi paper of the reform, and wrote books and pamphlets in plain Punjabi: stories, verse, and arguments about what the Gurus taught. Tradition remembers him in public debate too. Fourth, why his birth matters. In a hymn in Asa, Guru Nanak says to recognize the divine light in each person and not to ask about their caste, because caste counts for nothing hereafter. The Lahore reformers said all Sikhs are equal before the Guru, and Ditt Singh's own life put that teaching in plain view. Men of honored lineage sometimes sneered at his birth, and he answered them with his pen. In his story, learning isn't a family inheritance. It's open to anyone who sits down and does the work.

964.title: Professor Gurmukh Singh
964.hook: a teacher who pushed for Punjabi and Sikh education
964.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Professor Gurmukh Singh as a Lahore teacher and Singh Sabha leader who pushed for Punjabi in Gurmukhi and for Sikh education, and whose excommunication the Akal Takht later declared void.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Giani Ditt Singh, who earned his learning and answered sneers with his pen. Today, the friend who stood beside him.

A classroom in Lahore. Chalk on the board. The language of government is English, the language of the courts is Urdu, and the language of the students' own homes, Punjabi, barely has a place in school. Their teacher thinks that's a problem worth spending his life on. If Sikh children can't read Punjabi in the Gurmukhi letters, how will they read the Guru's word? He's a professor and a reformer, and his reforms will cost him.
screen: `A CLASSROOM IN LAHORE.` → `PUNJABI HAS BARELY A PLACE.` → `HOW WILL THEY READ THE GURU'S WORD?`

segments.voice: First, the classroom. Gurmukh Singh taught at Oriental College in Lahore, and pressed for Punjabi to be taught properly, in Gurmukhi, the script of the Guru Granth Sahib. A language that isn't taught in school slowly becomes a language only for the kitchen. Second, the organizer. He was among the leaders of the Lahore Singh Sabha, and worked to link the Singh Sabhas into a wider council. He started papers, gathered writers like Giani Ditt Singh, and argued for a Sikh college where young Sikhs could study modern subjects without losing their own tradition. Third, the price. His plain teaching on equality angered powerful men in Amritsar, including some of honored lineage. Priests there issued an edict casting him out of the Panth. He kept teaching anyway. Much later, the Akal Takht itself declared that edict void, restoring his name. The record was corrected, long after the man was gone. Fourth, what a teacher is in the Sikh tradition. The word Sikh, Sikh teachers explain, means a learner, a disciple, and the Gurus are teachers. The Guru's hymns speak of the true Guru as the one who joins the seeker to the Name. A human teacher isn't the Guru, but a good one points the way. Gurmukh Singh spent his life pointing young people toward their own language and their own scripture.
screen: `PUNJABI IN THE CLASSROOM.` · `LINKING THE SABHAS.` · `CAST OUT, LATER RESTORED.` · `SIKH MEANS A LEARNER.` · then, large: `THE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you know how to do well, a recipe, a song, a way of calming down, a few words of another language, and one person who might want to know it. 965.title: Khalsa College, 1892
965.hook: a Sikh college rises in Amritsar
965.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Khalsa College in Amritsar as a fruit of the Singh Sabha reform, built with gifts from Sikh princes and ordinary Sikhs, and it still teaches students today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Professor Gurmukh Singh, the teacher who wanted Punjabi in the classroom. Today, the college he argued for.

Outside Amritsar, on open ground along the road toward Lahore, a crowd gathers for a foundation stone. British officials in formal dress. Supporters from the Sikh princely states. Singh Sabha reformers, teachers and writers. And ordinary Sikhs who've given what they could, so that this could happen. Nothing stands there yet but a stone and a plan: a college where young Sikhs can learn science and English without being taught to leave their Gurus behind.
screen: `A FOUNDATION STONE.` → `PRINCES, REFORMERS, ORDINARY GIVERS.` → `A COLLEGE NOT YET BUILT.`

segments.voice: First, why a college. The Singh Sabha reformers had schools and papers. But young Sikhs who wanted higher study went to colleges run by the government or by missions, and some, as the reformers saw it, came back strangers to their own tradition. The reformers wanted a place that taught the modern subjects and Sikh learning under one roof. Second, who paid. Sikh rulers of the princely states gave large sums. The British government gave its support. And collections went around the Punjab, in towns and villages, from people with little to spare. The college belonged, in that sense, to everyone who put something in. Third, the name. Khalsa is the name Guru Gobind Singh gave the community of the initiated, those who belong directly to the Guru. A Khalsa College says what it's for: a college for that community, open to learning from anywhere, rooted in the Guru's word. Over time, a great building rose on that ground, and generations of students passed through it. Fourth, what the Gurus say about learning. In a hymn in Asa, Guru Nanak says that when learning is truly reflected on, the learned one becomes a help to others. Learning that stays in the head, or serves only pride, misses the point. The founders hoped the college would turn out graduates who served: teachers, doctors, writers and leaders who carried what they'd learned back into the Panth.

segments.voice: Choose one small thing you'd like to learn, a word of Punjabi, a line of a hymn, how a plant grows, the name of a street you walk down, and hold it as a question: breathe in curious, breathe out patient. Then ask who it could help once you know it, and let that person come to mind. If you pray, rest in Waheguru as the question settles.

966.title: We are not Hindus
966.hook: Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's book argued Sikhi was distinct, while honoring neighbors
966.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Ham Hindu Nahin as a scholar's case, built from the Gurus' hymns, that Sikhi is a distinct path, written with respect for Hindu neighbors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Khalsa College, built with gifts from princes and ordinary Sikhs. This week ran from pardesi through the Sabhas, Ditt Singh, Gurmukh Singh and a college. It ends with a book.

A book title can sound like a slammed door. This one, in Punjabi, is Ham Hindu Nahin: we are not Hindus. Read only the cover and you might expect an attack. Open it, and the author starts somewhere else. He's writing to his Hindu neighbors and friends with respect, he says, and he means them no ill will. He simply wants to set down, plainly, from the Gurus' own words, what makes the Sikh path its own. The author is Bhai Kahn Singh of Nabha.
screen: `A TITLE LIKE A SLAMMED DOOR.` → `OPEN IT: RESPECT FIRST.` → `BHAI KAHN SINGH OF NABHA.`

segments.voice: First, the question. In the years of the Singh Sabhas, a debate ran through the Punjab: were Sikhs a separate faith, or a branch of the wider Hindu family? Some Hindu reformers held that Sikhs belonged within the Hindu fold, and some Sikhs agreed. Other Sikhs disagreed sharply. Second, the scholar. Kahn Singh was a learned man from the princely state of Nabha, at home in Punjabi, Persian and the old texts. He answered not with insults but with quotations, page after page, setting the Gurus' hymns beside the claim. Third, his evidence. The Sikhs, he argued, have their own Guru, the Guru Granth Sahib; their own initiation, the Khalsa's amrit; their own rites for birth, marriage and death; their own places of worship. And he pointed to the Gurus themselves, including a hymn you met some days ago: Guru Arjan, in Bhairo, saying he is neither Hindu nor Muslim, and that his body and breath belong to the One whom some call Allah and some call Ram. Kahn Singh read it as the Gurus marking out a path of their own. Fourth, the kindness. In the Punjab, some Sikh and Hindu families were kin, sharing weddings, festivals and grief. Kahn Singh's book draws a line around the Sikh path, but it doesn't push the neighbors away. Hindus describe their own traditions in their own words; this lesson is about how one Sikh scholar said who his community was, while still sitting at a neighbor's table.
screen: `SEPARATE FAITH, OR A BRANCH?` · `A SCHOLAR'S ANSWER: QUOTATIONS.` · `OWN GURU, RITES AND PLACES.` · `A LINE THAT DOESN'T PUSH AWAY.` · then, large: `DISTINCT, AND KIND.`

segments.voice: Finish this sentence quietly, in your own words: I am someone who… and let one honest answer come: a faith, a practice, a value, a place you belong. Picture saying it to a neighbor who sees the world differently, with the same words but a warmer tone, and notice that the truth didn't change. If you pray, let Waheguru be the quiet you return to.
Kahn Singh, the scholar of Nabha who wrote Ham Hindu Nahin, setting out from the Gurus' words what makes Sikhi distinct, while honoring Hindu neighbors. Today's word.
Your line: distinct, and kind. A clear line, and an open door. Day nine hundred sixty-six, and the week closes.
